summary:
Saint Lucia's High Court decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct on 29 July 2025, striking down the colonial-era buggery and gross indecency offences as unconstitutional in Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia. Human Rights Watch reported the judgment on 31 July 2025, and the Associated Press covered it as part of a wave of strategic constitutional litigation across the Eastern Caribbean. For a visitor, criminal exposure for private consensual adult same-sex conduct ended with that declaration.

The Criminal Code No. 9 of 2004, in force since 1 January 2005, remains on the books as amended by the ruling. Section 132 defines gross indecency as genital acts other than intercourse for sexual arousal or gratification and carries ten years on indictment or five years on summary conviction, but exempts private consensual acts between adults. Section 133 defines buggery as anal intercourse and carries life imprisonment where committed by force and without consent, ten years otherwise, and five years for an attempt or assault with intent, exempting private consensual acts where both parties are 16 or older.

The Domestic Violence Act, passed on 8 March 2022, is the clearest protection available to a trans visitor or resident who is a victim of violence. It uses gender-neutral definitions of spouse, cohabitant, visiting relationship, domestic relationship, applicant and respondent, and its definition of domestic violence covers economic and sexual abuse, harassment, cyber-stalking, coercion, threats and intimidation. Clause 5 requires public officers and service providers not to discriminate on grounds that include sex, gender, sexual orientation and gender identity, and transgender victims and survivors have equal access to remedies, including court protection orders.

Enforcement and protection machinery has been the subject of targeted training. A human rights sensitisation session in 2014 instructed the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force on general and LGBT-specific content, and a further session in Castries on 19 May 2015 brought together officers from the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force, Air and Sea Ports, Customs and the Bordelais Correctional Facility with regional and international civil-society organisations. The 2015 programme built on the 2014 work.

Documented violence against sexual-orientation minorities includes the 2011 attack and robbery of three American gay men in a vacation villa, in which the assailants used anti-gay slurs, and the February 2019 stabbing murder of Michael Pooran, a 27-year-old Guyanese man, alleged to have been motivated by his perceived sexual orientation and followed by calls to denounce violence and revisit the buggery laws. In March 2019 the United Kingdom Upper Tribunal held that gay men are at risk of persecution in Saint Lucia and may claim asylum. No trans-specific violence data was identified.

Saint Lucia was the only UN member state in the Americas to formally oppose the UN declaration on sexual orientation and gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
The 2025 ruling formed part of strategic constitutional litigation across the Eastern Caribbean, in which courts in several jurisdictions have been asked to strike down colonial-era offences.

Before the ruling, the buggery and gross indecency provisions were documented as not enforced, with 2017 statements that no one had been imprisoned for being gay and that gay cruises, couples and visitors stayed safely. That enforcement record is the background against which the 2025 declaration was made.
localsOnly:
Article 131 of the Labour Code, enacted in 2006, bans unfair dismissal based on sexual orientation.

The Domestic Violence Act's gender-neutral definitions of spouse, cohabitant and visiting relationship extend its protection to unmarried and cohabiting partners, and its remedies, including court protection orders, are available to transgender victims and survivors on the same terms as other applicants.

In March 2019 a 17-year-old reported as openly gay, Gervais Emmanuel, died by suicide; the death was attributed to homophobic bullying and pressure.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust case digest for Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403), so the judgment's full reasoning is not sourced here.

No trans-specific violence data, no data on bathroom or facilities access rules, no data on gender-marker or document-change procedures, and no data on entry or visa screening specific to trans travellers were identified.

The 2011 and 2019 incidents are individual documented cases; no denominator or rate is available, so they cannot be used to rank Saint Lucia's risk level against other jurisdictions.
